# BLO-21857 — sweep run Secrets orphaned by a crash before the owner patch

This is the final text of the `PROVENANCE-CHANGES.md` row that
[#1459](https://github.com/Blockcast/paperclip/pull/1459) carried, moved here
verbatim, except for one corrected clause (the `list` blast-radius sentence,
aligned with the grant's comment in `deploy/helm/paperclip/templates/role.yaml`),
because that file is frozen (see [README.md](./README.md)): commits
appending to it are what got #1459 ejected from the rebase merge queue with
`merge_conflict`.

Changed files: `src/server/secret-sweep.ts` (new), `src/server/secret-sweep.test.ts` (new), `src/server/execute.ts`, `src/server/execute.test.ts`

Added a periodic sweep that collects run Secrets orphaned when the control plane crashes between `createNamespacedSecret` and the `ownerReferences` patch. Kubernetes GC only cascades through recorded owner references, and the Job `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` cascade is no different, so such a Secret is never collected — and since these carry credential material ([BLO-17973](https://paperclip.blockcast.net/BLO/issues/BLO-17973)) an orphan is a credential resident in etcd indefinitely, not litter. The sweep is deliberately conservative: it deletes only a Secret that is labelled ours with a non-empty `paperclip.io/run-id`, has zero `ownerReferences`, is past an age floor, and whose owning Job is absent by **both** the run-id label and the `<jobName>-<suffix>` name convention — with the name-derived Job re-read from the API server immediately before the delete, so a Job created after the list snapshot still saves its Secret. Absence must be *proven* by a 404; a read that succeeds, or fails for any other reason (throttling, RBAC, an old client), retains. **An earlier revision of this change stamped a renewable `launch-expires-at` lease on each Secret and raced the Job create against its renewals; that was removed (−350 lines) because it let a cleanup path fence and kill a healthy launch whose Job had already been created — a far worse failure than the orphan it was collecting.** The age floor replaces it using nothing but the object's own `creationTimestamp`, which needs no renewing, is identical from every replica, and survives a crash by construction. Two follow-up fixes from the Ally review at `e16bc908e`, both of which could lose a live run. (1) `ageFloorMs` is now clamped **up** to `MIN_SWEEP_AGE_FLOOR_SEC` (300s) rather than merely defaulted: `orphanSecretSweepAgeFloorSec: 0` reached the sweep as `0`, under which `now - createdMs < 0` is false for every Secret, so the three a live launch had just written became candidates — and because they are created *before* the Job exists, both Job checks and the pre-delete re-read miss. `?? DEFAULT` cannot catch an explicit `0`. (2) The gate is now wall-clock bounded at `DEFAULT_SWEEP_TIMEOUT_MS` (15s, matching the neighbouring pre-launch Job lookup): it already swallowed rejections, but **a hang is not a rejection**, and the call sits inside `execute()`'s per-agent creation mutex whose slot is released only by the `finally` at the bottom of the function — so a wedged `listNamespacedSecret` did not merely stall its own run, it held that agent's mutex for the process lifetime and blocked every later `execute()` for that agent. The bound lives in `createSweepGate` rather than the call site because the gate's contract was already "never fails a run" and "never hangs a run" is the same contract. The two bounds are deliberately **asymmetric** and the docstrings say why, so a later reader does not "fix" the inconsistency: a too-short timeout fails toward leaving orphans behind (recoverable, visible on the dashboard), a too-short age floor fails toward deleting live credentials (not recoverable). Only the second gets a hard clamp; `orphanSecretSweepIntervalSec` is left unclamped for the same reason, against an explicit reviewer suggestion to clamp both. **New RBAC, and it is a real widening — the first revision of this row claimed the opposite.** `delete` on Secrets and `get`/`list` on Jobs were already granted, but `list` on Secrets was **not**, so `deploy/helm/paperclip/templates/role.yaml` now adds it. Caught by the Ally review at `49412481`, which checked the live cluster rather than trusting the sentence: Role `paperclip/paperclip-k8s-adapters` granted exactly `create, delete, get, patch, update`. Without it the sweep 403s on its very first call, `createSweepGate` swallows that as non-fatal, and the feature is inert on every replica forever — and *invisibly* so, because a sweep that 403s and a sweep that finds zero orphans produce identical output and an identical flat gauge, which defeats the "fails toward leaving orphans behind, which is visible on the dashboard" fallback this row claims elsewhere. Unlike the `update` grant above, this one is not privilege-neutral: a Secret **list returns `data` for every match**, not just names. `get` was never name-restricted (this Role carries zero `resourceNames` clauses), so the SA could already read any Secret in the namespace whose name it could produce; what `list` adds is **enumeration** of names it could not have guessed, plus bulk retrieval of their `data` in one call instead of N. That is a genuine widening, but a narrower one than read access to values it could not otherwise reach, and it matches the comment on the grant in `role.yaml`. The sweep reads nothing but `metadata`, but the verb does not know that and the grant is what is audited. There is no narrower form — RBAC has no metadata-only verb and `resourceNames` does not apply to `list`. Pinned by a new `secrets:list` assertion in `deploy/helm/paperclip/tests/role-rbac.test.mjs`, alongside the existing `pods:delete` and `secrets:update` pins, both of which exist because the same silent-403 class bit in production before. Cleanup on the success path and both existing failure branches is byte-identical. All four guards were mutation-tested — reverted alone, each must turn the suite red. Worth recording that one of them did **not**: `falls back to the default bound rather than disabling it on a non-positive timeout` passed on broken code, because the harness mocks resolve as microtasks and so beat a `setTimeout(…, 0)` macrotask whether or not the guard existed. It asserted the right thing and could not catch its own defect; the listing now costs one real macrotask.
